# Volume 1 — CHAPTER XVIII. Nell to the Rescue

!!! note "Source text"
    Passages cited on the wiki pages link into this page. Only volumes at or before
    this page's cutoff are present.

EVERY great matter is intertwined with every small matter. On the surface, it may not appear that the choice made by a particular Canadian Premier regarding the addition of St. Brendan’s Island to a political tour could possess much or any connection to the fate of little Nell Harcourt at Grey Shutters. Nevertheless, it did.
{: #nw-v01-c18-p0000 }

The Premier arrived during one January so that he could speak to his devoted followers and whatever opponents selected to attend the enormous public gathering hosted in Port Marlow. Because the majority of Brierley residents shared the political party of the Premier, almost every man and a large fraction of the women traveled to the town thirty miles distant during the evening of the gathering. Mrs. Agatha Sowerby departed as well. Being a passionate partisan, Mrs. Agatha Sowerby was incapable of believing the political rally might succeed if she were absent, even though her political views were opposing. Consequently, she traveled to town, bringing along her spouse—Thomas would prove helpful by caring for the horse—as well as Thirza Abernethy. Having a secret fascination with politics on her own part, Thirza believed this could be her sole opportunity to view an actual living Premier, so she immediately seized the occasion, leaving Nell and Obed to watch over the home prior to her arrival back the next day.
{: #nw-v01-c18-p0001 }

Therefore, during the time that Thirza and Mrs. Agatha were having a wonderful time at the mass meeting, Nell and Obed were alone in the cozy kitchen at Grey Shutters. In the old-style Waterloo stove, a brilliant fire glowed, and frost crystals of a bluish-white color sparkled on the windowpanes. On the sofa, Obed was dozing over a Farmers’ Advocate, whereas Nell sat at the table and applied herself to her lessons with stubborn resolve, even though she cast several longing looks toward the clock shelf, which held a fresh book that Odette Pullen had provided her that very day. Odette had promised her that it was guaranteed to deliver countless thrills, or something along those lines, and Nell’s hands ached to grasp it. However, doing so would result in Hugh Carrow’s victory the following day. Nell rotated away from the clock shelf and attempted to pretend it did not exist.
{: #nw-v01-c18-p0002 }

“Did you ever learn geometry when you attended school, Obed?”
{: #nw-v01-c18-p0003 }

“Well now, no, I didn’t,” Obed remarked, abruptly awakening from his slumber.
{: #nw-v01-c18-p0004 }

“I wish you had done so,” sighed Nell, “since you would then have the capacity to sympathize with me. Proper sympathy is impossible if the subject has never been studied by you. My entire life is being darkened by it. Obed, I am such a dunce at it.”
{: #nw-v01-c18-p0005 }

“Well now, I dunno,” Obed said in a soothing manner. “I reckon you do well enough at everything. It was last week in the Delford store owned by Blair that Mr. Pidgeon mentioned to me that you were the school's brightest student and were advancing rapidly. ‘Rapid progress’ were the exact words he used. Some people disparage Teddy Pidgeon and claim he isn't much of an instructor, but I reckon he's fine.”
{: #nw-v01-c18-p0006 }

Whoever spoke well of Nell would have been considered “all right” by Obed.
{: #nw-v01-c18-p0007 }

“If only he wouldn't alter the letters, I’m sure geometry would be easier for me,” Nell complained. “After I memorize the proposition, he draws it on the blackboard using letters that differ from the ones in the book, which confuses me completely. Do you think it’s fair for a teacher to take a mean advantage like that? Agriculture is what we are studying now, and I’ve finally discovered the reason the roads are red. That brings me great comfort. I wonder if Thirza and Mrs. Sowerby are having a good time. According to Mrs. Sowerby, Canada is going to the dogs because of how things are managed at Ottawa, serving as a terrible warning to voters. She claims a blessed change would happen quickly if women had the right to vote. How do you vote, Obed?”
{: #nw-v01-c18-p0008 }

“Conservative,” Obed answered without delay. Supporting the Conservative party formed a component of Obed’s faith.
{: #nw-v01-c18-p0009 }

“Then I’m Conservative as well,” Nell stated with conviction. “I’m happy about it since Hughie—since a few of the male students at school are Grits. I suppose Mr. Pidgeon is a Grit as well because the father of Sukey Pullen is one, and Opal Pettigrew claims that a courting man must always share the same religion as the girl’s mother and the same political views as her father. Is that accurate, Obed?”
{: #nw-v01-c18-p0010 }

“Well now, I don’t know,” Obed remarked.
{: #nw-v01-c18-p0011 }

“Was there ever a time you went courting, Obed?”
{: #nw-v01-c18-p0012 }

“Well now, no, I reckon I never did,” uttered Obed, who assuredly had never contemplated such a matter throughout his entire life.
{: #nw-v01-c18-p0013 }

Nell thought carefully, resting her chin on her hands.
{: #nw-v01-c18-p0014 }

“Wouldn’t you agree that it must be quite fascinating, Obed? According to Opal Pettigrew, once she reaches adulthood she intends to keep a whole bunch of suitors dangling and drive every one of them wild over her; nevertheless, my own feeling is that it would prove excessively thrilling. My preference would be for merely a single one who remains sane. Even so, Opal Pettigrew is well versed in those topics on account of having a large number of older sisters, and Mrs. Sowerby remarks that the Pettigrew daughters have been snapped up rapidly like hot cakes. Almost every night, Mr. Pidgeon pays a visit to Sukey Pullen. His explanation is that he goes to assist her with her schoolwork, yet Ottilie Mott is likewise preparing for the Regent’s examination, and it seems to me her need for assistance is far greater than Sukey’s since she is considerably more foolish, yet he fails to visit her in the evenings to assist her whatsoever. This world contains a vast number of matters that I struggle to comprehend clearly, Obed.”
{: #nw-v01-c18-p0015 }

“Indeed, I am not sure that I grasp every one of them on my own,” Obed admitted.
{: #nw-v01-c18-p0016 }

“Well, I guess my lessons need to be completed. I will not permit myself to unseal that new volume Odette gave me to borrow before I am finished. However, it is an awful lure, Obed. I can view it right there just as clearly even if I rotate away from it. Odette mentioned that she wept until she was ill because of it. A book that causes me to weep is something I adore. Nevertheless, my thought is to transport that volume to the sitting room, secure it inside the jam closet, and hand the key over to you. Furthermore, you are forbidden from handing it back to me, Obed, prior to my lessons being completed, even in the event that I beg you on my knees. Declaring one should resist temptation is fine, but resisting it becomes far simpler when obtaining the key is impossible. Additionally, should I hurry to the cellar to retrieve a few russets, Obed? Would some russets appeal to you?”
{: #nw-v01-c18-p0017 }

“Well now, I don’t know but what I would,” stated Obed, who refrained from eating russets himself yet was aware of Nell’s fondness for the fruit.
{: #nw-v01-c18-p0018 }

Right as Nell stepped out of the cellar in triumph carrying her plate of russets, the noise of rushing feet on the frozen board walk outdoors was heard, and a second later the kitchen door flew open to admit Isolde Pembroke, who burst in pale and out of breath with a shawl thrown hurriedly over her head. Nell immediately dropped her plate and candle due to her shock, and the plate, candle, and apples tumbled all at once down the cellar ladder, where they were discovered at the foot covered in cooled grease the following day by Thirza, who picked them all up and expressed gratitude that the home had not caught fire.
{: #nw-v01-c18-p0019 }

“What on earth has happened, Isolde?” Nell shouted. “Did your mother finally change her mind?”
{: #nw-v01-c18-p0020 }

“Oh, Nell, do come quick,” Isolde begged anxiously. “Posy Fay is terribly ill—she has croup. Young Mary Joe says—and Father and Mother have gone to town and no one is available to fetch the doctor. Posy Fay is terribly bad and Young Mary Joe is at a loss as to what to do—and oh, Nell, I am so frightened!”
{: #nw-v01-c18-p0021 }

Silently, Obed took his coat and cap, glided by Isolde, and vanished into the yard's dark night.
{: #nw-v01-c18-p0022 }

“He has set off to hook up the sorrel mare so he can head to Delford to fetch the physician,” stated Nell, who was hastily putting on her jacket and hood. “It is as clear to me as if he had spoken it aloud. Obed and I share such a deep bond that I am able to discern his mind with no words whatsoever.”
{: #nw-v01-c18-p0023 }

“He won't catch the doctor at Delford, I'm sure,” Isolde wept. “Dr. Blair went to town, as I am aware, and Dr. Tranter likely went as well, I suppose. Nobody with croup has ever been seen by young Mary Joe, and away is where Mrs. Sowerby is. Oh, Nell!”
{: #nw-v01-c18-p0024 }

“Do not weep, Izzy,” Nell remarked in a cheerful manner. “I am fully aware of how to treat croup. It has escaped your mind that Mrs. Rudge gave birth to twins on three occasions. Caring for three sets of twins inevitably provides a person with extensive practice. Every one of them contracted croup at frequent intervals. Remain here briefly while I fetch the bottle of ipecac—it is possible you lack it in your home. Let us go at this moment.”
{: #nw-v01-c18-p0025 }

Clasping hands, the pair of young girls rushed forward, traveling along Linger Lane and then over the crusted field past it, since the excessive depth of the snow prevented them from taking the briefer forest path. While Nell felt genuine sympathy for Posy Fay, she remained fully attuned to the romantic nature of the circumstances and the joy of partaking in that melodrama again alongside a like-minded companion.
{: #nw-v01-c18-p0026 }

It was a clear, frosty night, filled entirely with the silver of snowy slopes and the ebony of shadows; above the quiet fields, large stars shone bright; scattered throughout, the dark, pointed firs rose up, their branches dusted with snow as the wind whistled amongst them. Nell felt that traveling smoothly across such mystery and beauty alongside the bosom friend who had been alienated from her for so long was genuinely wonderful.
{: #nw-v01-c18-p0027 }

At three years old, Posy Fay was truly extremely ill. Resting on the sofa in the kitchen, she was restless and running a fever, and the entire house echoed with her raspy breaths. Mrs. Pembroke had hired young Mary Joe, a healthy, wide-faced French girl from the creek, to look after the children while she was away, but Mary Joe was confused and powerless, entirely unable to figure out what needed to be done, or to execute it even if she did know.
{: #nw-v01-c18-p0028 }

Nell set about her task with deftness and speed.
{: #nw-v01-c18-p0029 }

“Posy Fay definitely has croup, and her condition is rather severe, though I have witnessed more extreme cases. Our initial requirement is a large quantity of hot water. Isolde, I swear the kettle barely contains a cup! Now that I have topped it off, Mary Joe, you can add wood to the stove. Without meaning to cause offense, it strikes me that an imaginative person would have anticipated this earlier. Next, I will remove Posy Fay’s clothes and tuck her into bed while you attempt to locate some soft flannel rags, Isolde. To begin her treatment, I intend to administer a dose of ipecac.”
{: #nw-v01-c18-p0030 }

Posy Fay did not react well to the ipecac, yet Nell’s experience in raising three sets of twins proved useful. That ipecac was swallowed, not just one time, but repeatedly throughout the lengthy, worrisome night as the pair of young girls attentively tended to the afflicted Posy Fay, while Young Mary Joe, sincerely eager to assist in any way possible, maintained a blazing fire and warmed a larger quantity of water than a hospital filled with croupy infants would have required.
{: #nw-v01-c18-p0031 }

Obed brought a physician at three o'clock, having found it necessary to travel as far as Tullyvale to secure him. However, the urgent necessity for help had elapsed. Feeling significantly improved, Posy Fay was resting deeply.
{: #nw-v01-c18-p0032 }

“Despair almost caused me to surrender,” Nell clarified. “Her condition steadily deteriorated until her illness surpassed that of the Rudge twins, even the final set. My belief was truly that choking to death would be her end. Every single drop of ipecac from that bottle was administered by me, and as the final dose was swallowed, I uttered to myself—avoiding Isolde and Young Mary Joe so as not to increase their existing anxiety, yet needing to speak it internally merely to ease my emotions—‘Upon this final remaining hope I rely, though I dread it is useless.’ Nevertheless, roughly three minutes later, she expelled the phlegm through coughing and immediately commenced recovering. Doctor, you have to envision my sense of relief, since expressing it verbally is impossible for me. As you are aware, certain matters defy verbal expression.”
{: #nw-v01-c18-p0033 }

“Yes, I know,” the doctor affirmed with a nod. He gazed toward Nell as though contemplating aspects of her that defied verbal description. Subsequently, though, he voiced these thoughts to Mr. and Mrs. Pembroke.
{: #nw-v01-c18-p0034 }

“The small red-haired girl living at Abernethy’s possesses as much intelligence as anyone could. I am telling you that the baby would have died before my arrival if she had not saved its life. A child as young as she is exhibits a degree of ability and composure that is truly remarkable. When she described the situation to me, her eyes were unlike anything I had ever witnessed.”
{: #nw-v01-c18-p0035 }

It was a marvelous, white-frosted winter morning when Nell headed back to her house, her eyes heavy due to a lack of sleep, yet she conversed tirelessly with Obed while they traversed the expansive white field and passed beneath the sparkling, magical arch formed by the maples of Linger Lane.
{: #nw-v01-c18-p0036 }

“Oh, Obed, isn’t this morning marvellous? It seems as though the world is something created by God purely for His own enjoyment, wouldn’t you say? Those trees appear so delicate that a single breath from me could blow them away—pouf! It makes me so happy to reside in a world that features white frosts, doesn’t it you? Also, I am very pleased that Mrs. Rudge ended up having three sets of twins. Had she not, I might have been at a loss regarding how to help Posy Fay. I truly regret ever being angry with Mrs. Rudge on account of her having twins. Even so, oh, Obed, I feel terribly tired. School is out of the question for me. I am certain I could not hold my eyes open and would act so foolishly. Yet I dislike remaining at home, because of Hughie—someone else will take the top spot in class, and climbing back up is so difficult—even if, naturally, the greater the difficulty, the more gratification one receives upon reaching the top again, don't you think?”
{: #nw-v01-c18-p0037 }

“Well now, I suppose you’ll get by fine,” Obed said, observing Nell’s pale small face as well as the dark circles beneath her eyes. “You simply go straight to bed and get some rest. I’m going to handle every chore.”
{: #nw-v01-c18-p0038 }

Nell consequently retired to bed, sleeping with such duration and depth that the pale, blushing winter afternoon was far advanced by the time she roused herself and went down to the kitchen, in which sat Thirza, having returned in the interim, engaged in her knitting.
{: #nw-v01-c18-p0039 }

“Oh, was the Premier seen by you?” Nell immediately blurted out. “Thirza, how did he look?”
{: #nw-v01-c18-p0040 }

“Well, his appearance prevented him from ever becoming Premier,” Thirza stated. “That man possessed quite a nose! However, he possesses speechmaking ability. Belonging to the Conservatives made me proud. Agatha Sowerby, who is a Liberal naturally, found him worthless. Nell, your dinner rests inside the oven, and from the pantry you may retrieve some blue plum preserve for yourself. You must be hungry, I suppose. Obed described last night's events to me. Truly, knowing how to act was lucky, I must admit. Having never witnessed a croup case, I would have lacked any idea what to do. There now, refrain from speaking until after you consume your dinner. Your appearance tells me you are simply overflowing with speeches, yet they can wait.”
{: #nw-v01-c18-p0041 }

Thirza possessed news for Nell, yet she withheld it at that moment because she recognized that sharing it then would cause Nell’s resulting enthusiasm to transport her completely away from practical concerns like her appetite or the meal. Thirza waited until Nell had consumed the last of her dish of blue plums before stating:
{: #nw-v01-c18-p0042 }

“Mrs. Pembroke came by this afternoon, Nell. Although she wished to speak with you, I chose not to disturb your sleep. According to her, you preserved Posy Fay’s life, and she deeply regrets her behavior regarding that currant wine incident. She mentioned that she currently realizes you had no intention of making Isolde intoxicated, and she trusts you will pardon her and resume your close friendship with Isolde. You have permission to visit her tonight if you wish, since Isolde is unable to step outside her home because of a severe cold she acquired yesterday evening. Now, Nell Harcourt, please do not lose your temper for goodness’ sake.”
{: #nw-v01-c18-p0043 }

The caution appeared far from unwarranted, given how elevated and weightless Nell’s demeanor and posture became as she leaped up, her countenance illuminated by the fire of her soul.
{: #nw-v01-c18-p0044 }

“Oh, Thirza, is it possible for me to leave this second—leaving my dishes unwashed? Upon my return, I will clean them, yet I am unable to bind myself to a task as devoid of romance as cleaning dishes during such an exhilarating time.”
{: #nw-v01-c18-p0045 }

“Indeed, indeed, off you go,” Thirza remarked forgivingly. “Nell Harcourt—have you lost your mind? Return here right now and wear some clothes. Calling out to the wind would be just as effective. Without a wrap or cap, she has departed. Observe her rushing across the orchard while her hair flows behind her. Should she avoid catching her death of cold, it will be a blessing.”
{: #nw-v01-c18-p0046 }

Nell arrived back home, dancing over the snowy expanses in the purple twilight of winter. Far off toward the southwest, a great evening star glittered like a pearl within a sky of pale gold and delicate rose, set above gleaming white areas and dark spruce glens. Through the frosty air, the sound of sleigh bells among the snowy hills tinkled like magical chimes, yet that music was no sweeter than the song Nell carried in her heart and on her lips.
{: #nw-v01-c18-p0047 }

“You behold a completely joyful individual in front of you, Thirza,” she stated. “I am completely joyful—indeed, regardless of my ginger hair. At this exact moment, my spirit transcends ginger hair. Mrs. Pembroke gave me a kiss and wept and mentioned that she was deeply apologetic and that she could not ever compensate me. I experienced intense embarrassment, Thirza, but I simply uttered as courteously as possible, ‘I bear no resentment toward you, Mrs. Pembroke. I guarantee you once and for all that my intention was not to make Isolde drunk and from now on I will drape the blanket of forgetfulness over what happened.’ That was a rather noble manner of talking was it not, Thirza?”
{: #nw-v01-c18-p0048 }

“It seemed to me as though I were piling burning embers on Mrs. Pembroke’s head. Isolde and I enjoyed a delightful afternoon together. She demonstrated a novel decorative crochet stitch that she had learned from her aunt in Delford. No one in Brierley besides the two of us is aware of it, and we made a serious promise that we would keep it a secret from everyone else. Isolde presented me with a lovely card adorned with a rose wreath and a poetic stanza:”
{: #nw-v01-c18-p0049 }

“Should you hold love for me equivalent to the love I hold for you, only death possesses the power to sever our bond.”
{: #nw-v01-c18-p0050 }

“And that is accurate, Thirza. We intend to request that Mr. Pidgeon allow us to sit side by side in school once more, and Tibby Tulk is able to accompany Posy Pullen. Our tea was splendid. Mrs. Pembroke arranged her finest china, Thirza, precisely as though I were genuine company. I am unable to describe the excitement it brought me. Prior to this, no one had ever brought out their finest china for me. Furthermore, we were served fruit cake, pound cake, doughnuts, plus two varieties of preserves, Thirza. On top of that, Mrs. Pembroke inquired whether I drank tea and remarked ‘Pa, why don’t you pass the biscuits to Nell?’ It has to be wonderful to be an adult, Thirza, considering that merely being handled like one feels so pleasant.”
{: #nw-v01-c18-p0051 }

“I am uncertain of that,” Thirza replied, letting out a short sigh.
{: #nw-v01-c18-p0052 }

“Well, regardless, once I reach adulthood,” Nell stated with conviction, “my conversation with young girls will constantly treat them as adults, and their usage of long words will never provoke my laughter. Personal, sad events have taught me how deeply such amusement wounds a person. Isolde and I prepared some taffy following tea. Our batch lacked quality, likely owing to the fact that it marked a first attempt for both Isolde and me. While Isolde buttered plates, she assigned the stirring to me, but I became distracted and allowed the mixture to scorch; later, as we placed it on the platform for cooling, a cat stepped across a single plate, forcing us to discard it. Nevertheless, we had a marvelous time preparing it. Afterwards, upon my return home, Mrs. Pembroke requested that I visit as frequently as possible, while Isolde remained by the window, blowing kisses toward me until I reached Linger Lane. Thirza, I guarantee that a desire to pray fills me this evening, and I intend to compose an entirely original, specific prayer to commemorate this event.”
{: #nw-v01-c18-p0053 }
